name: Giuseppe Garibaldi
role: Italian general and revolutionary, leader of the Expedition of the Thousand (1860) and Italian unification
summary: Garibaldi was a republican-minded nationalist and volunteer commander who fought for Italian unity and for liberal and republican causes in South America, Rome, Sicily, Poland-adjacent campaigns and France. He accepted Savoy monarchy as the means to unity, exercised a short dictatorship in Sicily and Naples, and was fiercely anticlerical, hostile to the temporal power of the papacy, and sympathetic to the International and later to peace and arbitration among free democracies.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: His Geneva proposition 3 said that every quarrel between nations would be judged by the Congress.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: He commanded the defence of Rome against French intervention in 1849, sent his Nullo Brigade to the 1863 Polish revolt against Russia, and led volunteers for republican France in 1870.

arms-reduction.rationale: His September 1867 letter said nations should spend on useful works rather than on cuirasses, bombs, mercenaries and spies.

clerical-rule.rationale: He fought the papacy's temporal power in 1849, 1862 and 1867 and in 1867 asked that the papacy be declared fallen from human institutions, wanting scientists and thinkers rather than priests as teachers.

conscription.rationale: His decree of 19 May 1860 from Salemi made all men aged 17 to 50 liable to militia service, in field, province or commune by age group.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: His 19 May 1860 decree from Alcamo abolished the tax on articles of food and every tax the Bourbon authorities had imposed since 1849.

death-penalty.rationale: Under his dictatorship in Sicily three death sentences were carried out, on a looter and on men convicted of murder and robbery, and he did not stop them.

democratic-peace.rationale: His 1867 proposition 10 said democracy alone can cure the scourge of war by overthrowing falsehood and despotism.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: His 1867 Geneva propositions made war between nations impossible and gave a congress of nations, one vote each, the judging of all their quarrels.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He praised Lincoln as the great emancipator in 1863, and his memoirs praise the freed slaves who fought as lancers in the Riograndense Republic.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: In his 1871 letter to Petroni he condemned a society where the few take most of what the many produce without having earned it by the sweat of their brow.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: His record points both ways: he served the Savoy king and ruled Sicily in his name, yet fought for the Roman Republic in 1849 and French republican forces in 1870, and told Mazzini a republic in 1860 would have been foolish.

national-self-determination.rationale: His career was fighting for national independence and unity (Italy, plus volunteers sent to Poland in 1863), which Campanella describes as dying for self-determination.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The 1879 League of Democracy programme he founded called for compulsory, free, lay primary education.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: In September 1867 he wrote that the confederation of all free democracies would advance slowly but surely, with a permanent universal association seated at Geneva.

priority-to-poor.rationale: As dictator at Naples in September 1860 he decreed twelve public infant asylums and, in Sicily, land quotas for propertyless poor families.

property-franchise.rationale: He backed universal suffrage, in 1860 plebiscites and in the programme of the League of Democracy he founded in 1879.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: He led the wars and expeditions that joined the Italian states, divided after 1815, into one kingdom, and kept pressing for Rome and Venetia after 1860.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: He proposed in 1867 that the Congress adopt the "religion of God", which he defined as the religion of truth and reason, and that members spread it.

strong-leader.rationale: As dictator of Sicily from May 1860 he rejected committees, insisting one man must head the government, and Crispi and Treccani describe him favouring temporary dictatorship in crises over parliamentarism.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: As dictator of Naples in September 1860 he abolished the Jesuits and declared their property national, and he supported abolishing religious orders in his later programme.

widespread-small-property.rationale: His 2 June 1860 Palermo decree gave poor heads of families without land a lot-drawn quota of communal or state land, with a double share for those who had fought.

notes: Searched all themes, including his decrees as dictator (taxes, land, asylums, Jesuits) and the memoirs. Sources and local corpus available were thin on economy, ecology, technology, gender and most government detail, so those stay null. His mature position on monarchy versus republic is mixed: he accepted the Savoy king in 1860 but remained republican in sympathy. Late League of Democracy items (death-penalty abolition, women's emancipation, standing army) rest only on secondary web pages I could not verify, so they are not used. His 1867 and later words on war and peace are not used where his campaigns give a record.
